project_announced_description: This Rural Development investment will be used to construct a new wastewater treatment plant for the Aspen Village Metropolitan District in western Colorado. The plant was constructed in the mid-1960s and consists of three interconnected lagoons with surface aerators. All three unlined lagoons perform the physical and biological treatment of the unscreened wastewater. It is unknown if sludge removal has ever occurred. Three active groundwater monitoring wells surround the lagoons and are monitored monthly for groundwater level fecal coliforms. The existing system is now beyond its useful life and does not meet current Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment (CDPHE) requirements since it does not include a disinfection process. This project will include the construction of a new Sequencing Batch Reactor facility near the current site. This solution will provide the community with the lowest cost alternative for wastewater treatment, with the least impact to the environment and the surrounding watershed. In addition, this project will decommission the lagoons. When complete, this project will provide the 600 residents of this rural community with modern, environmentally friendly wastewater treatment that meets all current CDPHE requirements.

project_announced_description: This Rural Development investment will be used to upgrade the wastewater treatment plant for the town of Yampa in the Rocky Mountains of Colorado. The town's current system was built in 1973 and has not seen meaningful improvement since 1982. It has not been meeting ammonia nor biochemical oxygen demand limits in recent years and has been experiencing more frequent violations. Total Inorganic Nitrogen is also of increasing concern. Beyond permit challenges, the lagoon liners and much of the mechanical equipment has reached the end of its useful life. The system also suffers from a lack of automation, telemetry and alarms requiring constant monitoring and manual adjustments along with work stoppages to diagnose any issue. This project will implement Membrane Bioreactor technology at the existing location consisting of two treatment trains. This will replace the current aging plant and lagoons and includes reclamation of the old lagoon sites with removal of biosolids. When complete, this project will ensure the 399 residents of this mountain town will have wastewater treatment that meets all regulatory requirements and is more cost-effective to run.

naics_industry_sector: Utilities
project_announced_description: This Rural Development investment will be used to upgrade the water treatment system for the town of Walsh in southeastern Colorado. The Town's current system is out of compliance for maximum levels for nitrates and radium in their drinking water and is under an enforcement order from the Colorado Department of Public Health & Environment (CDPHE). The system is served by only one well providing no redundancy in the event of a failure. Additionally, the system's meters have reached the end of their useful life and are providing inaccurate readings for water usage, resulting in lost revenue. This project will purchase an additional well east of the Town that is lower in nitrates and will allow for water to be blended with the existing well to improve quality. This project will also install an absorptive filtration system to further improve quality and bring the water system back into compliance. New water meters will be installed as well. When complete, this project will give the 543 residents of this rural Town access to potable water that meets all CDPHE requirements and allows for future expansion.

funding_code: (LOAN ONLY) WATER ONLY
naics_industry_sector: Utilities
project_announced_description: This Rural Development investment will be used to repair and replace the distribution system for Meadow Mountain Water Supply Company (MMWSC), serving a small community near Allenspark in northern Colorado.The current distribution system is over 50 years old and includes over 3.5 miles of a mixture of iron pipe and PVC buried at various depths ranging from 6 inches to 9 feet. Depth of burial is constrained by the depth to bedrock and certain sections of the water mains are subject to freezing during the winter months. To address freezing and bacterial growth issues due to infiltration from line breaks, MMWSC continuously bleeds the water mains in an effort to keep the water flowing. This results in over four times as much water being bled and wasted than is delivered to customers. Even with this ongoing bleeding operation, recent line freezing in February 2023 has left four residences without water.This project will replace the most problematic 40 percent of the current failing system with new raw water transmission mains, which will be buried at a greater depth (eight to 10 feet deep) than its current burial. A fire hydrant will also be installed into the raw water main. The project will also replace high pressure and medium pressure distribution mains. To minimize disturbance, the new distribution lines will be placed into the same trench but 18 inches to 2 feet above the raw water line in compliance with Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment requirements. Like the transmission line, the new distribution line will be laid at a freeze-protected depth of eight feet, thus reducing breaks and bacterial growth. Flow meters will be added to the raw water and finished water lines to ensure water balance between the intakes, plant and first customer. This project will also include the first steps towards connecting the system to Allenspark's water system for redundancy and increased firefighting capability.When complete, this project will ensure the 912 rural residents served by the Company have access to potable water delivered by a less wasteful system along with planning for the future and connection to Allenspark's system.

project_announced_description: This Rural Development investment will be used to replace the aging distribution system of the Sedalia Water and Sanitation District in central Colorado. Currently, the District's distribution system consists largely of undersized steel or asbestos cement pipes that are corroding, allowing frequent leaks, infiltration and inadequate fire flow protection. The system is not looped, creating areas where water stagnates and promotes bacterial growth. This phase of the project includes construction of the most critical items for the District. The portions of the water lines to be upsized as part of this phase were evaluated by the District and their consultants. They are locations with the highest frequency of breaks, locations that will loop the system and improve pressure, and lines with a large number of connected users. Remaining lines not meeting this criteria will be replaced as part of Phase 2. This phase will also allow for a future connection to nearby Castle Rock's water system for redundancy in the event of an emergency. When complete, this project will address the most critical needs for the 181 residents of this rural community until funds can be raised for the remaining phases of the project.

funding_code: (COMB LOAN & GRANT) WASTE DISPOSAL ONLY
naics_industry_sector: Utilities
project_announced_description: This Rural Development investment will be used to construct a new wastewater treatment system for the town of Bethune in eastern Colorado. The system was initially constructed in 1977 and consists of two non-aerated lagoons with authorization to discharge effluent into groundwater. Currently, only one lagoon is used while the other remains empty. The town was issued a new discharge permit certification by the Colorado Department of Public Health & Environment (CDPHE) in February 2019; however, the existing facility cannot meet the requirements outlined in the permit including effluent limits (no treatment exists), seepage limits (neither lagoon is lined), nor the sampling & monitoring requirements (no upstream or downstream monitoring wells or flow measurement). This project includes the construction of a complete retention/evaporative pond system that meets all current CDPHE design standards to contain all wastewater from the Town of Bethune's service area as well as an influent screen and splitter structure. This will eliminate the discharge from the facility and bring the town into compliance with CDPHE regulations. All ponds will be lined with synthetic liners to meet CDPHE seepage regulations. The project also includes the decommissioning of the existing treatment plant including biosolids removal, and the construction of a 3-pond evaporative system. When complete, this project will ensure the 183 residents of this rural Town have access to wastewater treatment that is in compliance with all regulations and is sized appropriately for their service area.

funding_code: FY22 CONGRESSIONALLY DIRECTED SPENDING
naics_industry_sector: Public Administration
project_announced_description: This Rural Development investment will be used to construct a Community Justice Center in Lake County in western Colorado through Congressionally Directed Spending. The Lake County Jail, which operated below capacity for decades, was closed in April 2019 due to critical safety and security issues. The closure of the jail requires all detainees to be transported to jails in other counties. The jail closure has proven costly to the community, particularly during COVID-19 restrictions. The county has spent hundreds of thousands of dollars to operate without a jail since 2019, and those detained are lodged far from family, employers and legal counsel. Conditions within Lake County Courthouse are equally pressing. The facility lacks security and privacy for victims, witnesses, court staff and the public, and with only one courtroom, pandemic-related backlogs have pushed both civil and criminal hearings back months. In 2022, Lake County purchased a ~10.5 acre undeveloped parcel of land just off Highway 24 at the entrance to Leadville with the intention of building a Community Justice Center that includes a courthouse, police stations and detention center. Fentress Architects has provided plans with an estimated cost of $54m for the entire project. The County is evaluating its options, including perhaps phasing the project to bring the immediate cost down. These Congressionally Directed funds will be used to help construct the selected alternative. When complete, this project will bring down the long-term cost to the 7,436 residents of this rural community by bringing these government functions back into their area along with improving conditions for all involved.

naics_industry_sector: Utilities
project_announced_description: This Rural Development investment will be used to improve the water system for the town of Holly in Southeastern Colorado. The current system is supplied by three wells and is under an enforcement order from the Colorado Department of Public Health & Environment (CDPHE) for being out of compliance for maximum levels of radium in their drinking water. The 100,000-gallon storage tank is undersized, providing inadequate fire flow and less than a day's worth of storage. The distribution system has several dead ends allowing for bacterial growth, utilizes undersized and older asbestos cement and cast-iron mains resulting in water loss and infiltration. This project will construct a new well adjacent to the treatment building to replace two of the older wells. The new water treatment plant designed to bring the town into compliance with all regulations will also be next to a new 450,000-gallon storage tank that can supply a full day's demand and provide 2 hours of fire flow. Additionally, by replacing the undersized pipes and eliminating dead ends in the system, water loss will be reduced, and water flow will be improved. When complete, this project will ensure the 837 rural residents of Holly have reliable access to potable water and fire protection that fully complies with CDPHE requirements.

project_announced_description: This Rural Development investment will be used to improve the wastewater treatment facilities (WWTF) and collection system for the town of Silverton in southwestern Colorado. The current facilities consist of two separate but connected systems: a wastewater collection system and a three-cell aerated lagoon WWTF, including a lift station and dewatering well. The dewatering well has been inoperable for four years, the lift station's components have reached the end of their useful life, and the lagoon liners are failing in many locations and need repairs. On the collection side, many sections of pipe and manholes need to be rehabilitated or replaced. This project will install a new pump house and improve monitoring of the lift station to reduce the risk of catastrophic failure and environmental damage, rehabilitate the existing dewatering well to return it to operation and spot repair the lagoon liners. The project will also include replacing sections of the collection system piping and manholes to reduce inflow & infiltration thereby reducing the volume the plant needs to treat. When concluded, this project will ensure the 717 rural residents of Silverton have reliable wastewater treatment with a lower risk of environmental damage for years to come.

funding_code: COMMUNITY FACILITY (DIRECT AND GUARANTEED LOANS)
naics_industry_sector: Health Care and Social Assistance
project_announced_description: This Rural Development investment will be used to renovate and expand the main campus of the Wray Community District Hospital in eastern Colorado. Since opening its doors in the current facility in 1995, the District has opened a Primary Care Clinic, added to imaging by providing a CT Scanner and mobile MRI and completed an addition for larger cardiac and therapy departments. However, since the pandemic, the District's patient load has increased dramatically as neighboring facilities cut back on offered services. This project will expand the additional hospital's footprint by roughly 13,500 square feet, providing updates to the Surgery Department, Imaging / Womens Care Center, Ambulance Bay, On-call Rooms, Staff Locker Rooms, and the Primary Clinic. It will also provide a new Surgery and Emergency Department Entry and relocate the Helipad. The existing building will be renovated to reorganize the layout with the new space and update the Emergency Department. When complete, this project will ensure the 2,342 rural residents coming from as far away as Kansas and Nebraska have access to the care they need.

funding_code: FY22 CONGRESSIONALLY DIRECTED SPENDING
naics_industry_sector: Manufacturing
project_announced_description: This Rural Development investment will be used to remodel the food preparation area for Fort Lewis College in Durango, located in southwestern Colorado. The colleges existing facility does not meet their operational needs, as it does not provide the appropriate food storage, a designated prep area, and is not Americans with Disabilities Act accessible. This project will include a grocery-style pantry that includes a food prep area and a resource hub. In addition to providing free healthy groceries, the center will also offer support resource navigation services such as the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program registration. In the past year, the college experienced a 233 percent increase in usage and a 427 percent increase in food distribution. The proposed design will allow the college to maximize food storage capacity, and provide areas for community-building and interaction. Additionally, the center has been intentionally placed near two established organizations that support Native American and Latino populations. Given that Fort Lewis College is primarily a Native American-serving non-tribal institution with more than 50 percent students of color, the project will help reduce existing inequalities and create a new model for addressing food security and rural agricultural development in the region. This project will ensure the 16,501 Durango rural area residents have access to the essential food pantry that can accommodate the growing demand for its services.

funding_code: CF ARP EMERGENCY RURAL HEALTH CARE GRANTS - TRACK 1 & 2
naics_industry_sector: Manufacturing
project_announced_description: This Rural Development investment will be used to provide immediate relief from the effects of the COVID-19 pandemic for La Puente Home, Inc., a non-profit that runs a soup kitchen in the San Luis Valley of southern Colorado. Prior to the onset of the pandemic, the kitchen served approximately 23,000 meals a year using dishes and silverware that were cleaned and sanitized between use. Meals were served in the kitchens cafeteria which seated 70 diners. Implementing COVID-19 protocols including the use of foam to-go containers, plastic water bottles and plastic silverware that allowed the kitchens visitors to take their meals with them presented a substantial cost. In addition, supply chain issues also increased the cost of the kitchens bulk ingredients. This project will help offset these unexpected costs and allow La Puente Home to continue serving meals to those in need in this rural community of 8,780 residents.

funding_code: CF ARP EMERGENCY RURAL HEALTH CARE GRANTS - TRACK 1 & 2
naics_industry_sector: Other or Not Defined
project_announced_description: This Rural Development investment will be used to provide immediate relief from the effects of the COVID-19 pandemic for the Food Bank Network operated by La Puenta Home, Inc., a non-profit in the San Luis Valley of southern Colorado. The Food Bank Network worked diligently to provide a stable presence for households struggling with the various crises arising from the pandemic. Substantial funding was expended on cleaning supplies and masks to further local public health safety goals. During the pandemic onset, their food supplies dwindled due to shortages from local donors and nationwide wholesale partners. Additional food was required to meet the increased demand for services and equipment and it was difficult to find funding for facilities to store the added food volume. This project will assist the Network to cover unexpected expenses and continue supplying nutritious foods to food-insecure residents. This will also lead to a decrease in medical costs, as food insecurity has significant impacts on health outcomes. It will allow the Network to continue their important mission of providing food to residents in the San Luis Valley, a rural region of 8,780 residents.

funding_code: CF ARP EMERGENCY RURAL HEALTH CARE GRANTS - TRACK 1 & 2
naics_industry_sector: Health Care and Social Assistance
project_announced_description: This Rural Development investment will be used to perform renovations to improve patient and staff conditions at the San Luis Valley Regional Medical Center operated by the Lutheran Hospital Association of the San Luis Valley in southern Colorado. The Regional Medical Center dates back 100 years and only offers significantly overcrowded, semi-private rooms with non-American Disability Act (ADA) compliant bathrooms for inpatient care. This leads to concerns regarding infection prevention, isolation of contagious pathogens, privacy and overall patient experience as well presenting challenges to staff attempting to care for these patients. This project will convert seven rooms, presently used for outpatient cardiopulmonary services, into flexible private suites, including two that will have negative-pressure heating, ventilation and air conditioning systems for enhanced infection control and isolation capabilities. All rooms will feature ADA-compliant bathrooms, LED lighting, air scrubbers and necessary technology updates for modern equipment and patient monitoring. It will also fund updates and new equipment for the nursing station that serves these rooms. Overall, this project will improve the level of care and pandemic resilience for this medical facility serving 8,780 rural residents while also alleviating the largest source of patient complaints about the current conditions.

project_announced_description: This Rural Development investment will be used to improve and modernize the water treatment facility for Montezuma County in southwestern Colorado. Currently, the system can handle four million gallons per day. Some of the equipment dates back to the construction of the facility in 1985 and expansions in 1999 and 2009 that increased capacity to its current level, though it is insufficient for the current population and will only become more so given the projected population increase in the area. Several health and sanitary concerns exist with the current facility, including possible contamination of filtered water. This project will expand the plants capacity to six million gallons per day with possible future expansion to eight million gallons. It will install new water pumps, a new redundant treatment train including pretreatment, filtration and disinfection, new chlorine storage that allows for significantly reduced chlorine deliveries, a new, more robust pH adjustment system and new finished water pumps to increase capacity and conveyance.

project_announced_description: This Rural Development investment will be used to fund the necessary first steps for the town of Ovid in northeastern Colorado to upgrade its drinking water system. The towns water distribution system dates back to 1927 and though a portion was replaced in 2006, the rest of the system is still serviced by nearly 100-year-old transmission lines. The towns system is currently comprised of a single operational well equipped with a 40-year-old pump that is beyond its useful life. The eventual failure of this pump will force the Town to use their manually-operated backup well, only capable of an inadequate 65 gallons per minute at most. As of September 2021, the Towns disinfection system has failed as well, forcing them to use a temporary connection and borrowed pump. This project will fund the crucial first step of a Preliminary Engineering Report and Environmental Report so that the town can identify affordable alternatives to upgrade their water distribution system and ensure the 318 residents of this rural community have continued access to high quality drinking water.

project_announced_description: This Rural Development investment will be used to construct a non-traditional skilled nursing facility in the City of La Junta, serving a rural community of 18,830 residents in Southeastern Colorado. The former skilled nursing facility closed in 2020, forcing the areas residents to relocate to other facilities scattered throughout Colorado. The La Junta City Council commissioned a study and determined the area could support at least a 50-bed facility. Citizens of La Junta overwhelmingly voted to form the La Junta Health Service District and authorized a sales tax to make the facility a reality. This project will construct a new Green House or hybrid skilled nursing facility called Bluestem Village. The non-traditional facility will consist of four identical, stand-alone skilled nursing units with 14 beds per unit and a fifth building to include an administrative office and attached gathering area/community center. The development of an open, suburban site will include parking, sidewalks, landscaping, courtyard and walking paths on 35 acres of previously undeveloped land. The location is both close to the City and allows for future expansion (need is expected to rise to 117 beds in the future). Overall, this project will ensure the areas residents can live in their community and provide quality, skilled nursing care to the community going forward.

project_name: FY2020 REAP RES SOLAR PV REPLA
funding_code: REAP-MANDATORY RENEW ENERGY SYST GRANTS
naics_industry_sector: Agriculture, Forestry, Fishing and Hunting
project_announced_description: This Rural Development investment will be used to install a 84 kW roof mounted solar PV system. This system will produce 137,305 kWh annually, will offset 100% of this agricultural producers annual electric usage and is estimated to reduce their annual costs for electricity by an estimated $13,000 annually. The project is equivalent to offsetting the annual electrical usage of 13.4 homes. The purpose of this funding program is to assist farmers, ranchers, and rural small businesses in developing renewable energy systems, and in making energy-efficiency improvements to their operations.
